name: Mountain folk
one_line: They never had metal and never missed it: volcanic glass for a knife, burnt lime for a house, fitted stone for a wall that outlives its builders, and goats where nothing can be planted.

needs: a slope of loose stone, a crag or a lava flow within reach

staples: wild goat and marmot from the crags
roots and berries at the treeline
grass seed threshed like grain on the lava
how: the herd up to the high grass in summer, down in winter
the spear on the crags; a snare at the burrow
gathering below the treeline; a stew boiled in the hot pool where there is one
preserve: hard cheese dried in the wind
meat dried in thin cold air
a stone larder dug under the wall, cold all summer

fuel.note: branch and brush from the treeline; pine and larch logs where the slope still has them; above the trees only the herd's dung, dried on the wall (no herd, no fire up high); a lava field has brush and dwarf willow and little else; a hot spring cooks with no fuel at all

shelter.form: low houses of double-skinned dry stone packed with earth, a turf roof roped down against the wind, the goats under the far end of the same roof; whitewashed inside once the kiln has burned; a stone fold beside

ALPINE_MEADOW.fuel: branch and softwood from the treeline below; dung on the high pasture
ALPINE_MEADOW.food: milk and cheese, marmot and wild goat, bilberries and roots at the treeline
ALPINE_MEADOW.shelter: dry-stone huts with turf roofs at the treeline; a summer hut and fold up on the grass; the kiln where the rock is limestone
ALPINE_MEADOW.palette: meadow green, grey scree, lichen yellow, whitewash, snow

VOLCANIC_FIELD.fuel: brush and dwarf willow, dung; little wood, so no kiln: the lime comes up from the meadow camps by exchange
VOLCANIC_FIELD.food: pioneer berries (sea buckthorn, the lava bilberry), fireweed shoots, grass seed, fern pith in a hard year, goats on the first grass
VOLCANIC_FIELD.shelter: black lava blocks laid dry, turf roofs, no plaster; the obsidian flow is here and so is the knapping floor
VOLCANIC_FIELD.palette: black lava, red cinder, rust and map lichen, fireweed pink, obsidian glint

HOT_SPRING.fuel: the warm ground does half the fire's work: branch from the birch and pine, and the pool for cooking
HOT_SPRING.food: food boiled in the hot pool, cattail root, fish and wildfowl where the water cools, milk
HOT_SPRING.shelter: dry stone on warm ground, a bath cut in the sinter, a winter refuge for the whole slope; where the crust is travertine the kiln burns it
HOT_SPRING.palette: white and rust sinter, orange and green mats, steam, dark pine

knows: gentian root, the bitter tonic; alpenrose, the poison
dwarf juniper for smoke and flavour
sea buckthorn and fireweed on the lava
which hot pool cooks and which scalds
plantkeeper.teaches_flavour: why the goats leave the alpenrose alone; why a different flower grows on the kiln rubble; edelweiss is a token, not a cure
plantkeeper.teaches_practical: gentian root for a sick stomach; alpenrose is poison to eat; juniper smoke keeps flies off the fold; a coloured mat means the water is too hot

makes: quicklime, slaked to mortar and whitewash

techniques.name: Knapping
techniques.verb: strike a core of obsidian or flint with a hammerstone; the flake comes off with an edge a few nanometres thick
techniques.teaches: stone gives you a knife long before it gives you metal: sharper than a surgeon's scalpel, brittle, made in a minute; every flow has its own chemistry, so a blade found three hundred miles away names the volcano it came from
techniques.unlocks: the player knaps a knife: dress a carcass, cut cordage; the knapping floor glitters for ten thousand years

techniques.name: Lime
techniques.verb: stack limestone and wood in a stone-ringed pit, burn it a day and a night to quicklime, slake it with water
techniques.teaches: what turned a dry-stone hut into a house: mortar, plaster, whitewash that throws the fire's light back; five loads of wood for one of lime, so the kiln is the mountain's hunger
techniques.unlocks: the camp's plaster and whitewash; the kiln ring is the ruin

techniques.name: Dry-stone walling
techniques.verb: two faces, hearting between, through-stones tying them, the wall leaning in as it rises, copes on top; no mortar
techniques.teaches: fitted well, a wall stands five hundred years and shrugs off an earthquake; fallen, it reads as a ridge under the moss
techniques.unlocks: houses, folds and terraces; the camp's shelter ceiling

techniques.name: Terracing
techniques.verb: step the slope behind dry-stone risers so the soil stays and the water walks down
techniques.teaches: a plot on a hillside, and hay for the goats' winter
techniques.unlocks: a crop plot and a hay plot on a slope; terraces gone to bramble read as ridges (ruin)

techniques.name: The goat herd
techniques.verb: follow the wild goats, then keep them: a fold of dry stone, the kids brought in, the milkers kept and the young males eaten
techniques.teaches: the herd began on a mountain: a goat climbs where nothing can be planted and turns scrub into milk, hair, hide, tallow and fuel; it also eats the forest's children, which is the whole restraint of this life
techniques.unlocks: the camp's herd ceiling: milk and cheese, dung for the fire above the trees, tallow for the light (built last in the engine)

techniques.name: Rushlight
techniques.verb: peel a rush from the spring's edge to its pith, draw it through melted tallow, wedge it in a split stick
techniques.teaches: the herder's light: a stem and a thumb of fat, half an hour of flame, made by the dozen
techniques.unlocks: a short, cheap light to set down inside a shelter; any rendered fat serves, and the herd's tallow makes it by the handful

wants: salt (for the cheese and the goats)
hide, cordage and resin for hafting

ladder: fire in the lee of a dry-stone wall
the fold and the goats on the high grass: the herd
cheese in the cold store; the kiln burns and the hut becomes a house
blades go down the mountain and salt comes up
growth.restraint: the herd is kept below what the meadow regrows and off the saplings at the treeline (a goat eats the forest's children, and a slope stripped of young trees has no wood in a generation); the kiln burns only in a year with wood to spare; a quarry face never heals, so blades are struck thin and the cores worked to the last flake
growth.ceiling_hint: the herd is the fundamental built last in the engine, so until then a mountain camp stays a handful on forage and knapping and the kiln and the terrace wait; with the herd, an alpine meadow with a treeline reaches the tribal ceiling, and a lava field or a hot spring stays a small camp on a trade road

signatures.what: a glitter of black and grey flakes underfoot, a carpet of them, where nothing grows
signatures.restore: cleared: the new knapper sits where the old one sat
signatures.inherits: the cores and big flakes still cut: a camp's first knives come off the old floor

signatures.what: a stone ring sunk in the hillside, burnt red inside, a spill of white lime and ash below it
signatures.inherits: a kiln that draws from the first burn; whitewash a season sooner

signatures.what: long ridges under the moss where dry-stone walls came down; a stretch still standing where the through-stones held
signatures.restore: restored: the camp rebuilds on the old footing
signatures.inherits: the stone is already quarried and carried: walls go up in a season

signatures.what: steps in the slope gone to bramble; risers of stone under the roots
signatures.restore: restored: risers rebuilt, the steps come back
signatures.inherits: level soil that held for centuries: a plot the first spring

signatures.what: a ring of low wall too small for a house, the ground inside it greener
signatures.inherits: a pen ready for the herd, the day the herd exists

ruin.plants_differ: lime-loving plants on the kiln and the mortar rubble (thyme, rock-rose, saxifrage) in a meadow whose acid ground grows alpenrose and gentian; nothing at all on the flake floor; nettles on the old fold where the dung lay; the terraces hold deeper soil and grow taller than the slope

aesthetic.silhouette: low stone houses with roofs weighted by stone; a ring fold; a kiln smoking on the hillside; a goat standing on a wall
sounds: the click of the knapper's hammerstone

real_world.analogue: Anatolian obsidian (Göllü Dağ, the Kaletepe workshop, Çatalhöyük)
real_world.note: an open-air blade workshop among the oldest known; its glass reached Syria and Cyprus, up to 700 km off; Çatalhöyük, some 160 km away, knapped almost all its tools from Cappadocian obsidian; each flow's chemistry (XRF) names the volcano a blade came from

real_world.region: Kermanshah, central Zagros, Iran, c. 8200 BCE
real_world.note: the earliest evidence of goat domestication: almost no adult males in the bone, young males eaten and females kept to breed, a managed herd ten thousand years ago on a mountain

real_world.region: Jordan and the Levant, c. 7500–6000 BCE
real_world.note: lime plaster on floors and walls, renewed every few years, and statues of plaster on reed cores; burnt lime was a floor binder long before it was mortar; a heavy fuel cost for a town at the steppe-forest edge that later shrank as its land degraded

real_world.region: Yucatán and the Puuc hills, c. 600–950 CE
real_world.note: about five volumes of wood burnt for one of lime; stucco, mortar, plazas and nixtamal all needed it; stone-ringed pit kilns at Kiuic cut the fuel by a fifth, a conservation technique, and the ring is what survives

real_world.analogue: Inca masonry (the walls only; the Andes are highland folk)
real_world.note: ashlar fitted without mortar by hammerstone alone, walls leaning inward, trapezoid doors; in an earthquake the blocks dance and settle back; the fine work was for temples, the rest fieldstone and adobe

real_world.region: the Alps and Pyrenees, from c. 3000 BCE
real_world.note: herds driven to the high pastures every summer since the Neolithic; without the grazing most meadows below 2,000 m would be forest; the art of dry-stone walling was inscribed by UNESCO in 2018 (Switzerland, Spain, France and Italy among others)

real_world.region: Scottish Highlands and Islands, roofed into the 1970s
real_world.note: double dry-stone walls packed with earth, a turf-and-straw thatch, no chimney, the fire in the middle and the animals at the far end under one roof

real_world.region: Rotorua, Aotearoa New Zealand, since c. 1325
real_world.note: a village on geothermal ground for seven centuries: the hot pools and steam cook, bathe and heat the houses to this day
